ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
In vacuum, an electron performs uniform circular motion with a radius of r around a fixed point charge $^{+\mathrm{Q}}$, and the equivalent circular current of the electron is $\operatorname{I_1}$; two point charges, each with a charge of ${+Q}$, are separated by a distance r. A point A is located on the perpendicular bisector of their connecting line, and the distance from point A to each charge is also r. After obtaining an initial velocity perpendicular to the plane of the paper, an electron at point A can perform uniform circular motion around the midpoint O of the connecting line of the two charges, and the equivalent circular current of the electron is $\operatorname{I_2}$.

1. Determine the ratio of $\operatorname{I_1}$ to $\operatorname{I_2}$.

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: In vacuum, an electron performs uniform circular motion with a radius of r around a fixed point charge $^{+\mathrm{Q}}$, and the equivalent circular current of the electron is $\operatorname{I_1}$; two point charges, each with a charge of ${+Q}$, are separated by a distance r. A point A is located on the perpendicular bisector of their connecting line, and the distance from point A to each charge is also r. After obtaining an initial velocity perpendicular to the plane of the paper, an electron at point A can perform uniform circular motion around the midpoint O of the connecting line of the two charges, and the equivalent circular current of the electron is $\operatorname{I_2}$. ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: There are two schematic diagrams in the figure. Fig. 1 shows a fixed positive point charge +Q located at the center of a circular orbit, with electron e on the circumference, and the radius of the circle labeled r. Fig. 2 shows two identical positive point charges +Q located at the left and right ends of a horizontal dashed line, with the midpoint being O; point A is above the perpendicular bisector of the connecting line, and electron e is located at A; the distances from A to the left and right +Q are both labeled r, forming an equilateral triangle, and the vertical distance from A to O is the orbital radius. Reasoning: In Fig. 1, the Coulomb attractive force provides the centripetal force: kQe/r^2 = mv1^2/r, so v1 = sqrt(kQe/(mr)). The equivalent circular current is I1 = e/T1 = ev1/(2πr). In Fig. 2, the distance between the two +Q is r, and the distance from A to each +Q is also r, so the triangle is an equilateral triangle, and the radius of the circular motion of the electron around O is R2 = AO = (sqrt(3)/2)r. At point A, the magnitude of the attractive force of each +Q on the electron is kQe/r^2, the horizontal components cancel each other, and the components along AO pointing toward O add together. The component of a single force along AO is (kQe/r^2)(AO/r), so the resultant force F2 = 2(kQe/r^2)(AO/r) = 2(kQe/r^2)(sqrt(3)/2) = sqrt(3)kQe/r^2. From the centripetal force formula F2 = mv2^2/R2, we get sqrt(3)kQe/r^2 = mv2^2/[(sqrt(3)/2)r], so v2^2 = (3/2)kQe/(mr), that is, v2 = sqrt(3/2)v1. The equivalent circular current in Fig. 2 is I2 = ev2/(2πR2). Therefore I1/I2 = [ev1/(2πr)]/[ev2/(2πR2)] = (v1/v2)(R2/r) = sqrt(2/3)·sqrt(3)/2 = sqrt(2)/2.
